EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 13 Oct 2026 08:00:33 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Listen: Could the EU shield the ICC from US sanctions? https://euobserver.com/242416/listen-could-the-eu-shield-the-icc-from-us-sanctions/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 08:00:33 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242416 The United States has imposed new sanctions on the International Criminal Court, this time targeting the institution itself. The EU, while supportive of the ICC, does little to counter the sanctions.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

The United States has imposed new sanctions on the International Criminal Court, this time targeting the institution itself. While the EU insists on its firm support for the ICC, it is still not using the one tool designed for this kind of situation: the blocking statute.

So, why is the EU holding back? First, a quick reminder of what we’re talking about. The International Criminal Court, or ICC, is based in The Hague. It tries people accused of the gravest crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.

With one important limit: It can act when a crime is committed on the territory of a state that is party to the Rome Statute, or by one of that state’s nationals. The United States is not a party. Neither is Israel or Russia.  

Read more

‘Bullies cannot be appeased’: Pressure mounts on EU to shield ICC from new US sanctions

And Washington’s goal is clear: dismantling the court. The Trump administration considers it politicised and without legitimacy.

It is particularly opposed to the arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. That’s why, since 2025, the US has imposed several rounds of sanctions, targeting judges and, more recently, the court’s president, the Japanese national, Tomoko Akane.

On Friday, Washington went a step further, targeting the court as an institution.

So what does that mean in practice? All of the court’s assets in the United States are frozen. And, crucially, American companies and citizens can no longer provide services to the court or its members.

You might remember the case of the ICC judge Nicolas Guillou, who has been under sanctions for some time. We’ve talked about him in a previous Briefed episode.

Read more

Listen: How does the EU defend itself against US arbitrary sanctions?

He has explained that he can no longer use basic services such as Mastercard, or online platforms like Airbnb. He has also been warning that these sanctions are meant to intimidate, and that they undermine judges’ independence.

In a state governed by the rule of law, judges must not be put under pressure. This explains why the court’s reaction is so strong. It speaks of an obstruction of justice and an attack on the rule of law. And it is now calling on its members to take concrete action to protect its independence.

In response, the European Commission and the European Council have expressed their support for the court and its work. But without going too far.

They say the EU is ready to take measures so that the court can keep functioning. Yet when the Commission is asked what those measures are, and this has happened several times in recent months, it sidesteps the question.

Because beyond negotiations and diplomatic pressure, there is a tool created for precisely this kind of situation: the so-called blocking statute. It protects Europeans against the extraterritorial reach of sanctions imposed by third countries.

Read more

EU leaders to speak no evil of Israel, as Nobel prize recalls Gaza ‘genocide’

It doesn’t concern American actors. It concerns European companies and individuals who, under the threat of secondary sanctions, may become overly cautious.

In the case of the ICC, it’s about the court’s European banks, insurers and service providers.

Several European countries have called for the blocking statute to be activated. Yesterday, at the Foreign affairs council in Luxembourg, the Belgian and Dutch ministers asked the Commission to start analysing whether to do so.

But for now, they are still waiting for an answer. The Commission believes the priority is to use the six months before the sanctions take effect to negotiate with Washington, possibly to get them withdrawn.

This approach was backed by several EU foreign ministers yesterday. Let’s see whether that window for dialogue is enough, or whether the pressure to activate the blocking statute keeps growing.

]]> Poll shows public revulsion on caged hens ahead of EU-ban deadline https://euobserver.com/242365/poll-shows-public-revulsion-on-caged-hens-ahead-of-eu-ban-deadline/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 07:01:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242365 In a poll of 25,080 adults across 25 EU member states, 75 percent of Europeans indicated support for a hen-cage ban by 2035.]]> More than half of Europeans believe hens should no longer be caged, according to new data released on Tuesday (13 October). 

And 75 percent of Europeans wanted the last hen in the EU out of its cage by 2035 at the latest, according to a poll conducted by Savanta on behalf of Humánny pokrok, an animal rights non-profit.

Pollsters asked 25,080 adults across 25 member states for their views on keeping hens in cages.

The results show that 16 percent of people were not sure when or if putting hens in cages should be banned, while 7 percent of Europeans supported hen-caging until at least 2045.

The survey comes five years after 1.4 million citizens signed the European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) to ‘End the Cage Age’ and the European Parliament voted to endorse it.

‘Now is the time’

“This data shows millions of Europeans care about animal welfare,” said Barry Andrews, an Irish Renew MEP.

“Over 1.4 million signed the ECI, which was also supported by MEPs. Now is the time for the Commission to finally make a legislative proposal,” he added.

The delay in tabling legislation came after Copa Cogeca, a farming lobby group, insisted that banning hen cages could take up to 15 years.

But the new data says 52 percent of Europeans wish a hen cage ban was already in place.

Read more

Protesters in Brussels press EU on ‘broken promises’ over caged animals

The country most supportive of a hen cage ban was Austria, where 65 percent of people believed the last hen should have already left its cage, and 2 percent said cages for hens should never be banned.

Thomas Waitz, an Austrian Greens-group MEP, said an EU ban on animal cages is “long overdue” and urged Olivér Várhelyi, commissioner for health and animal welfare, to deliver an “ambitious timeline”.

“This long period of indecision is not just an affront to the European consumers who want better Animal Welfare, it also harms European farmers and producers who need reliable information for their investments,” Waitz said.

In Bulgaria, the member state which polled as least supportive, 33 percent of people believed the last hen should have already left its cage whereas 9 percent said cages should never be banned.

]]> Europe’s skills passport is missing a page, EMPASS wants to add it https://euobserver.com/242377/europes-skills-passport-is-missing-a-page-empasswants-to-add-it/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242377 Employers are reporting skills bottlenecks because CVs and qualifications often fail to capture skills they are looking for. Europe needs bridges between education and employment.]]>

This article is paid for by JA Europe.

On 15 September, the European Commission proposed a Skills Portability Act, a regulation designed to make qualifications digital, comparable, and easier to recognise across borders. It forms part of the Fair Labour Mobility Package and must still be adopted by the European Parliament and the Council before any of its measures can take effect. 

It is a welcome step. But it leaves open a question that deserves more attention in Brussels: what happens to the skills young people develop every day but their diplomas and CVs do not capture? 

Communication, teamwork, critical thinking, adaptability and resilience shape how people work with others and keep learning throughout their careers. Employers say they need these skills. According to the Commission’s 2023 Flash Eurobarometer, 74 percent of small and medium-sized enterprises reported shortages affecting at least one job role. Meanwhile, Eurostat found that in 2024 only 56.4 percent of people aged 15–34 in the EU with medium or high educational attainment reported a high or very high match between their field of education and the requirements of their current or last main job. 

These figures measure different things and should not be read as pointing to a single cause. Together, though, they show that having qualified people and having the right capabilities in the right place are not the same thing. Young people build those capabilities in classrooms, vocational training, volunteering, creative projects and first jobs. Yet they struggle to show them in a form that an employer, particularly one in another country, understands and trusts. 

The stakes are not abstract. In 2025, 11 percent of Europeans aged 15–29 were neither in employment nor in education or training. Skills recognition cannot resolve that on its own, but stronger links between learning and work are part of the answer. 

In effect, we are asking young Europeans to cross borders with incomplete passports. 

This is where micro-credentials can make a difference if they are built with credibility in mind. JA Europe coordinates EMPASS (Employment Skills Pass), an Erasmus+ Forward-Looking Project co-funded by the European Union. It brings together education providers, industry partners and Junior Achievement organisations to develop and validate an employability micro-credential covering 11 employability skills, from communication and teamwork to resilience and critical thinking. 

The micro-credential was designed to be piloted with 1,500 students in Greece, Romania and Spain. According to the project’s latest monitoring figures, 2,700 young people now hold an EmPass certificate. 

Beyond the pilot, the EMPASS approach is already demonstrating potential for wider uptake. The methodology has informed implementation and exploration activities in other countries, including Ukraine and Lithuania, and has been incorporated into wider youth employability initiatives such as the Global Alliance for Youth mentoring programme. This suggests that employability micro-credentials can be integrated into different learning and workforce-development contexts while maintaining a common framework for skills recognition. 

A micro-credential does not replace a diploma, and no single certificate can capture everything a person brings to a job. Its value lies in complementing formal qualifications with clearer, validated evidence of what someone can do. The aim should not be another certificate that employers overlook. 

Europe does not need more initiatives that show promise but struggle to reach scale. It needs bridges: between education and employment, between national systems, and policy ambition and lived experience. That means asking practical questions. Can a young person show the same verified capabilities to employers in different countries? Can employers see what microcredential assesses and how it was validated? Can schools and universities build it into existing pathways without adding administrative burden? 

The answers will decide whether skills portability becomes opportunity or remains a policy ambition. They are also the focus of From Skills to Opportunity, a JA Europe forum in Brussels on 14 October, bringing together policymakers, employers, educators and youth organisations, including speakers from the European Commission, the World Employment Confederation and the European Vocational Training Association. 

As the Skills Portability Act moves through parliament and council, Europe has a chance to put employability skills into the conversation from the start: not only how qualifications are recognised, but how capabilities developed through formal, non-formal and experiential learning can carry meaning across borders. 

Employability skills are not an abstract policy debate. They are part of the foundation for participation, mobility, and opportunity in Europe’s labour market. The task now is to ensure that every young person carries a passport that employers recognise, wherever their learning and career take them.

]]> France, Greece, and Netherlands see steep fall in crisis-resilience, study finds https://euobserver.com/242285/france-greece-and-netherlands-see-steep-fall-in-crisis-resilience-study-finds/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 22:01:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242285 With one in five adults worldwide hit by disasters in the past five years, millions of people in Greece and France could be dangerously exposed when the next natural or man-made crisis strikes.]]> More than a third of people who receive warnings of disasters are unable to act before they strike, according to a global poll. Social resilience has fallen also in Poland, Greece, and France.

The findings, published by the Lloyd’s Register Foundation on Tuesday (13 October), drew on more than 143,000 interviews conducted by Gallup across 140 countries in 2025.

They show that an estimated 1.1 billion people – one in five adults worldwide – experienced a disaster in the previous five years.

Almost 220 million received no warning at all.

“A warning is only as good as what people are able to do with it,” said Nancy Hey, director of evidence and insight at Lloyd’s Register Foundation’s Global Safety Evidence Centre.

The gap between being warned and being able to respond is stark between rich and poor countries. Adults in low-income countries were almost twice as likely to have been affected by a disaster as those in high-income countries, at 31 percent compared with 16 percent.

Yet only 64 percent of affected adults in low-income countries received a warning, against 84 percent in high-income countries.

Even when warnings arrive, they do not guarantee safety.

The challenge is not simply to warn people when disaster approaches, but to ensure they have the means and support to act.

Fewer than half of warned adults in low- and lower-middle-income countries were able to act, compared with 71 percent in high-income countries.

Europe’s resilience is unequal

The report’s companion study, ‘A resilient life: How wellbeing shapes the capacity to cope’, pictures the preparedness to act under pressure — including in wealthier countries.

“There are some changes that are happening in Europe that I’m not seeing in other parts of the world,” Hey told EUobserver.

Read more

Europe’s summer of wildfires puts spotlight on economic cost of climate inaction

Across the EU, 77 percent of people affected by a disaster received a warning, compared with 80 percent globally.

But only 59 percent of those warned could act, against 64 percent worldwide and 71 percent in high-income countries.

“Some of the biggest drops globally have been in Greece, Netherlands, Estonia, and France, which is surprising given that generally that measure is going upwards,” Hey said.

Just 29 percent of EU households have a disaster plan, and only 28 percent of people think their national government is well prepared for a disaster.

Meanwhile, 44 percent say their government does not care about them at all, compared with 29 percent globally.

The differences between countries are stark.

In France, 80 percent of those affected received warnings, but only 61 percent could act. Just 22 percent of households have a disaster plan, compared with 47 percent in Germany and 60 percent in Austria. And overall, France’s social resilience has fallen six points since 2021.

Greece faces a deeper crisis of preparedness and confidence.

Only 55 percent of disaster-affected people received warnings, and just 39 percent of those warned could act. Only 12 percent believe their government is well prepared, while 70 percent say it does not care about them.

]]> MEPs don’t have to meekly accept an EU budget deal, but will they go to war over €141bn in cuts? https://euobserver.com/242366/meps-dont-have-to-meekly-accept-an-eu-budget-deal-but-will-they-go-to-war-over-e141bn-in-cuts/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242366 MEPs and the champions of EU integration point to the parliament's co-decision powers as proof of the institution's importance. But will MEPs dare use those powers in a budget fight with governments?]]> Getting co-decision powers on the budget, finally enshrined in the Lisbon Treaty after more than a decade of inter-institutional battles, was one of the European Parliament’s big wins. 

The challenge facing MEPs in the coming months is whether they are really going to use those powers on the 2028-34 budget. 

The early signs are that they are spoiling for a fight. The Irish government’s compromise proposal tabled on Saturday (10 October) – an 8 percent cut worth €141bn to the European Commission’s spending plan – isn’t exactly butchery. 

But it does display a startling lack of ambition, in particular on the raft of ‘own resources’ proposed by MEPs to make the budget process less vulnerable to member states wanting to reduce or at least freeze their annual contributions  

This time round, MEPs have proposed a digital services levy, an online gambling levy, and a levy on crypto-asset capital gains.

Put together the parliament reckons that these new taxes could bring an additional €30bn to the EU’s budget, on top of the €57.4bn that the EU commission believes can be raised from other levies, such as the emissions trading scheme and the carbon border levy.

]]> [Interview] Spanish socialist MEP sees no other leader than Sánchez, as housing and immigration dominate snap election https://euobserver.com/242337/interview-spanish-socialist-mep-sees-no-other-leader-than-sanchez-as-housing-and-immigration-dominate-snap-election/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:03:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242337 Some 23 percent of Spain’s working population were immigrants, who were “paying taxes and [contributing to] pensions for everyone," said the MEP, ahead of a snap election dominated by its housing crisis and the Ceuta migrant crisis. ]]> “The issue is, do we have another leader to replace Pedro Sánchez?”.

Former Spanish congresswoman Hana Jalloul Muro is among her prime minister’s closest allies in the European Parliament.

“It has not been an easy mandate. Every day is a survival day, all the challenges that prime minister Pedro Sánchez has faced have been unprecedented,” the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) MEP told EUobserver.

They had faced the Covid pandemic, a volcanic eruption in the Canary Islands in 2021, and the migrant crisis in the Ceuta enclave in north Africa in the summer of 2026, she said – not to mention the corruption allegations levelled at his close relatives.

And he now risked being unseated in a snap election on 5 October, called after nationwide protests against lack of affordable housing.

Read more

Spain’s 54-day sprint to the polls: can Sánchez’s housing gamble stop the far-right from entering into government?

Sánchez’ PSOE party is trailing behind the centre right people’s party (PP) in the polls, which is also growing closer allied to the increasingly successful far-right Vox party. 

“These elections will pit two models against each other,” Jalloul said.

“On the one hand, a progressive government that defends public services, improves wages and pensions, expands rights and protects the social majority. And on the other, a model represented by the PP and Vox, which, wherever they govern, have opted for privatisations and policies that risk widening inequalities,” she said.

Ceuta-linked election

Jalloul, who spoke to EUobserver at the European Parliament (EP) in Brussels, used to lecture on international terrorism at the University of Madrid, before she became vice-chair of the EP’s foreign affairs committee.

And she recalled the heated debate on the Ceuta incident on 31 July, including accusations that Morocco had engineered it to gain leverage over Spain. 

Read more

Sánchez and the EU have decided that Morocco relations are too big to fail

“This is a crisis that we could not expect,” she said.

But had there not been a “good relationship with Morocco, [we] would never be able to return 90 percent of the 70,000 people that came in less than 72 hours,” she added.

]]> Forged news of military conscripts in Kaliningrad had hallmarks of a Western counter-attack in Putin’s info wars https://euobserver.com/242265/forged-news-of-military-conscripts-in-kaliningrad-had-hallmarks-of-a-western-counter-attack-in-putins-info-wars/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:45:35 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242265 Western spymasters may finally be testing Kremlin-style information tricks on Russian soil to rattle Putin’s war regime.]]> A lethal plume of toxic smoke was blowing towards us from a blaze at a battery manufacturing plant in Kaliningrad.

Troops in the Russian exclave had been ordered to help put the fire out: untrained and under-equipped, they mutinied. Terrified civilians were thronging the borders.

The Kremlin, oblivious to the unfolding humanitarian and environmental catastrophe, blamed the West for sabotage and incitement, and demanded a transit corridor across Lithuania.

However, none of this actually happened.

We (20 retired and serving officials, experts, and others) were in the safety and comfort of the Wargaming Lab at the ISM university in Vilnius, as guests of the Baltic International Security Centre (BISC).

The crisis scenarios were hypothetical; the aim was to explore the dilemmas and trade-offs they created. (You are the Lithuanian government. Do you let the mutineers in? Or leave them to be massacred?)

The games-master provided regular “injects” – new developments – such as ill-written social media posts from US president Donald Trump. He blamed the authorities in “Lithvastonia” for having started the fire in “Kaliningradia”.

An amusing parody, we thought. A few hours later, the real US president published news of his deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin on sanctions-busting diesel imports, then blamed Ukraine for being invaded.

Not so amusing, especially for our Ukrainian participant, a senior military commander there.

As we were leaving (us to safety, him to danger), news broke that Russia is stepping up its assassination attempts in Europe, targeting defence industry bosses (and perhaps Polish politicians). Our scenarios seemed tame in comparison.

]]> Tanks vs. drones battle exposes lie in Russia’s map of territorial gains, as Ukraine once again bombs Yandex data centres (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,691) https://euobserver.com/242324/tanks-vs-drones-battle-exposes-lie-in-russias-map-of-territorial-gains-as-ukraine-once-again-bombs-yandex-data-centres-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1691/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:43:36 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242324 Drones are now deciding who survives on the battlefield — and even which side's maps or propaganda can still be believed.]]>
  • They looked like Russian “porcupines” and fought where the Kremlin considers Russian rear territory. They were protected by their own drone.
  • Drones also struck Yandex’s third data centre.
  • The battle for Dobropillia on a new type of map.

  • Maps of the day — Dobropillia, Kharkiv region

    • They looked like Russian “porcupines” and fought where the Kremlin considers Russian rear territory. They were protected by their own drone. Both the Russian and Ukrainian armies are continuing their efforts to return tanks and combat vehicles to the battlefield.

    Russia recently attacked near Dobropillia with tanks fitted with upgraded Arena-M active protection systems.

    First, how do Europe’s gas reserves work? EU countries fill underground gas storage sites during spring and summer, when demand is lower, and draw on these stocks during the winter, when heating pushes consumption up.

    Since 2022, the EU has required member states to ensure their gas storage facilities reach 90 percent of capacity by a deadline between 1 October and 1 December. That helps secure supplies ahead of winter.

    That said, a colder or longer winter than expected, or disruptions to supplies in other parts of the world, could put additional pressure on the market. Especially at a time when the EU is preparing to phase out Russian gas imports in 2027.

    The EU has adopted a gradual ban, with transitional arrangements for existing long-term contracts.

    And Russian gas still accounted for around 12 percent of EU gas demand through May 2026. Imports even increased in the first months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, amid disruptions to energy flows linked to the war in the Middle East.

    Until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Czech Vanadium was among the European companies which clearly had Russian owners.

    Since 2007, the company has been controlled through the Evraz group by Russian businessman Roman Abramovich, who is close to Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

    The ferrovanadium producer was part of a chain through which vanadium ore mined in Russia reached Europe before being sent on to Abramovich’s factories in the US. Ferrovanadium is an alloy added to steel to help improve its properties. And Czech Republic accounts for six percent of global production.

    But sanctions following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 forced the oligarch to sell up.

    Evraz, the holding company in which Abramovich is the largest shareholder, supplied the Russian army, according to media reports. But Evraz denied this.

    In 2024, the Abu Dhabi-based company Metco (now ‘Metco Holding’) became the sole shareholder in the Czech factory, but it is not clear who controls it.

    Czech authorities and police suspect the transfer of the vanadium factory to a new parent company in the UAE may conceal the true owner. They are seeking to establish who is really behind the opaque company in the Persian Gulf, and whether it is still Roman Abramovich.

    Read more

    Top Russian oligarch Abramovich loses third EU lawsuit, as Brussels plans tougher blacklist

    According to Deník N sources familiar with the investigation, specialists from Czech police bodies for organised crime (NCOZ) and the financial intelligence unit (FAÚ) are involved.

    “Yes, we are investigating who is behind the company. There are many leads and the suspicion is clear that the company may still be backed by its former owners from Russia,” a source close to the investigation confirmed.

    NCOZ spokesperson Jaroslav Ibehej declined to comment in more detail on the search for Czech Vanadium’s beneficial owner. “As a rule, we neither confirm nor deny what we are working on,” he said.

    According to documents in the Czech judicial database, the company is formally controlled by one owner — a Dubai-based lawyer of Indian origin who provides nominee services for beneficial owners. The lawyer has been linked to money-laundering investigations in Ukraine and Moldova.

    Apparent fake owner scheme

    The officially declared owner of Czech Vanadium is Nikhil Skariah Kolekunnel. According to the ADGM free zone business register in the UAE, he is both the sole shareholder and director of Metco Holding.

    However, the Gulf state’s database does not disclose so-called beneficiaries, who are entitled to the company’s profits and may also secretly control it.

    Although the Czech judicial register lists Skariah as Czech Vanadium’s beneficial owner, this does not necessarily indicate the person exercising control in the background. For example, trustees of trust funds are also listed in the registers as beneficial owners.

    The nature of Skariah Kolekunnel’s business suggests that he performs the specific role of an administrator, a so-called fiduciary — someone who accepts an ownership mandate and effectively manages another person’s assets.

    He is a lawyer originally from India who founded two law firms in the UAE years ago. His companies represent large corporations and businesspeople who do not wish to publicly acknowledge ownership of a business.

    “South Bridge Legal is an advisory firm for comprehensive business establishment in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and the UAE. Our highly experienced team has been active in the sector for more than 10 years, providing services tailored to the unique needs of every ambitious entrepreneur setting up companies in Dubai,” the company wrote on its website.

    “We have all activities, which is tax management, tax consulting, accounting, corporate services, offshore company formation, free zone company formation…everything,” Skariah said in a recently published video on YouTube.

    Metco Holding’s address in Abu Dhabi suggests it may be a shell company. And it is headquartered from a WeWork.

    Moldova and Ukraine links

    ‘Skariah’, the name of the Indian administrator, had already emerged eight years ago in connection with the concealment of ownership structures during an investigation into the privatisation of Moldova’s national airline. At the time, Skariah appeared as the owner of the opaque company Gold Craft FZE, established in Dubai in 2015.

    “On Monday 1 October 2018, one day before the privatisation agreement for Air Moldova was signed, a plane from Istanbul landed at Chișinău International Airport. One of the passengers, a 39-year-old man, was carrying nearly €2.6m in cash in his luggage. He declared the money to customs officers, which, according to the Office for the Prevention and Fight against Money Laundering, he had borrowed four days earlier from Gold Craft FZE in the United Arab Emirates,” the investigative outlet RISE Moldova reported.

    It finds that Andrei Ianovici brought cash from Dubai, equivalent to tens of millions of Czech crowns. Later that day, he deposited the money in a bank, and it ended up in the accounts of Civil Aviation Group SRL. That company privatised Air Moldova, and Ianovici was one of its partners.

    The true origin of the money was never established, leading local investigators to suspect that the money had not been earned legally. No charges were brought, however.

    According to court records, Skariah was also involved in disputes in Ukraine, where Gold Craft FZE claimed ownership of an Ilyushin aircraft which the company allegedly purchased in 2017.

    Skariah’s Russian-linked empire

    However, the UAE-based lawyer was not the only individual to have emerged as an administrator of Czech Vanadium. Another is Sergei Gushchin.

    A man of this name was formerly a prominent Russian businessman in rail freight transport and, although he withdrew from Russia three years ago, he appears on Ukrainian sanctions lists for supporting the Russian army.

    Gushchin became a senior manager at PJSC TransContainer, a Russian rail freight carrier, after Evraz sold its stake. In the past, a quarter of the company was owned by the holding company of Abramovich.

    Meanwhile another of Gushchin’s companies, Rail Service, formed a joint venture with Evraz in 2019 focused on the production of railway wheels.

    According to a UAE register, Gushchin was a director and shareholder of Metco, which became Czech Vanadium’s parent company from 2022-23.

    US credit-rating agency Moody’s shared data with Deník N that listed Gushchin as a recent beneficiary of Metco Holding and as the company’s director.

    Russia’s ferrovanadium monopoly

    Czech Vanadium’s revenues regularly exceed €81m, and in 2024 the company reported profits of more than €8m. This summer, the company sent over €0.6m of that sum to the Dubai company, the remaining funds staying in its retained earnings account.

    Last year, the company recorded a modest €0.2m loss. Its accounts retained more than €12m in undistributed profits in total.

    Czech Vanadium’s business remains closely tied to Russia. Last year alone, vanadium oxides or hydroxides worth nearly €82m were imported into the Czech Republic from the Russian Federation. Russia is effectively the sole supplier of the raw materials needed to produce ferrovanadium. According to the statistical office database, exports mainly go to the United States, as well as Germany and Taiwan.

    Czech Vanadium did not reply to requests for comment or an explanation of its ownership structure.

    It also did not answer the question of how a Dubai lawyer had bought the Czech company, which, according to some estimates, is worth more than €40m.

    Company representatives have not responded to questions about its owners since 2024, when the company left the Evraz group structure.

    Fake owner model in US

    Jiří Skuhrovec, an analyst at Datlab, specialises in the global vetting of business partners. He says Abramovich uses a similar model for concealing ownership in the United States.

    Sanctions also forced the Russian oligarch, who became better known through his former ownership of the British football club Chelsea, to withdraw from US companies. But Skuhrovec concluded that they were probably still controlled by people linked to Abramovich just like the factory in Czech Republic.

    “We mapped the entire chain, from the Russian ore supplier through the Czech smelter to the final recipient: the US company Strategic Alloys LLC. Until recently, all three companies officially belonged to Abramovich, and all three are now controlled by people with links to his Evraz group. Abramovich may therefore still secretly control the entire supply chain for this strategic raw material. This would be a textbook case of sanctions circumvention, as well as an obvious security risk,” Skuhrovec said.

    Findings led Datlab and Transparency International to submit a complaint to police. “We believe that the 16m Czech crowns (around €655,000) in distributed profit may have gone to Abramovich, who is on a sanctions list. That would constitute a criminal offence,” the analyst explained.

    In brief:

    • Czech Vanadium, owned by Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich’s holding company until 2024, was taken over by Dubai-based company Metco Holding.
    • The company is opaque, and Czech authorities are investigating who actually owns the Czech factory. It is suspected it is still linked with former owner.
    • This would amount to circumventing sanctions imposed by the European Union.
    • Deník N and Datlab analyst Jiří Skuhrovec found that the company is backed by lawyer Nikhil Skariah Kolekunnel and Sergei Gushchin, who conduct business with Abramovich’s Evraz group.
    • Skariah has been linked to money laundering in Moldova and Ukraine. He has long covered for companies that are in fact owned by someone else.

    “The little man carries the big man, and the big man tells him: ‘Oh, I really want to help you. I really love you, but I do not want to get off your back.’ It is also a story about hypocrisy and double standards, which I combined,” the artist said.

    He covered the sculpture in gold because Trump is known to like the precious metal.

      <title>Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/12/nobel-prize-for-economics-hall-woodford-new-keynesian-models</link>
      <description><p>US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/12/uk-growth-inflation-pressures-oil-price-sveriges-riksbank-nobel-prize-economic-sciences-awarded-latest-news-updates">Business live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p>Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.</p><p>Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/advanced-economicsciencesprize2026.pdf">developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”</a>, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/12/nobel-prize-for-economics-hall-woodford-new-keynesian-models">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/11/trump-russia-diesel-deal-putin-little-impact-prices</link>
      <description><p>Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/11/zelenskyy-trump-ukraine-russia-energy-ceasefire">Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’</a></p></li></ul><p>Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian-diesel-ukraine">infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy</a> when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/11/trump-russia-diesel-deal-putin-little-impact-prices">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan</link>
      <description><p>‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’</p><p>Back through political history to the age of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ronald-reagan">Ronald Reagan</a>, Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers.</p><p>The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">artificial intelligence</a> pixie dust. It will fail again.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>AI surveillance startup Flock to cut several hundred jobs amid backlash, sources say</title>

      <description><p>Company, which grown rapidly in recent years, has been under scrutiny as privacy concerns grow</p><p>Flock Safety plans to shed about 18% of its employees, people with direct ⁠knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">AI</a>-powered <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/surveillance">surveillance</a> cameras and license-plate readers faces <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/25/florida-warrants-flock-camera-greg-steube">mounting opposition</a> to its products from communities and ⁠lawmakers.</p><p>The people said the job ⁠cuts came after ​a voluntary buyout program and were expected to affect roughly 270 employees at Flock, a surveillance technology startup that has seen rapid growth in recent ⁠years.       <title>Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/trump-investigate-lisa-cook-fed-governor</link>
      <description><p>US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional</p><p>Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/29/supreme-court-trump-lisa-cook-ruling">a June supreme court ruling</a> that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.</p><p>Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-immigration-cost-social-security</link>
      <description><p>New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034</p><p>Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/series/ice-2-0-inside-trumps-new-immigration-dragnet">anti-immigration campaign</a>, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.</p><p>Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-immigration-cost-social-security">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax</link>
      <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A <a href="https://no645.com/our-coalition/">coalition</a> of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 13 Oct 2026 08:57:13 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Irish house price inflation slows as affordability constraints bite ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/house-price-inflation-slows-as-affordability-constraints-bite/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/house-price-inflation-slows-as-affordability-constraints-bite/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Irish house price inflation slowed to a three-year low of 3.9 per cent between July and September as affordability pressures and higher interest rates weighed on demand.

That’s according to the latest survey from property website MyHome, which is owned by The Irish Times Group.

It found that asking prices nationally declined by 1.4 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months.

The company said “affordability remains stretched” with the median (middle value) sold price for properties listed on its website now at €412,000. This was 7.7 times average annual pay of €54,000.

The Irish property market is undergoing something of a reset in the face of higher borrowing costs, persistent supply shortages and changes to the rental rules.

David McWilliams: The numbers in the Irish housing market don't add up

MyHome’s latest barometer, compiled in conjunction with Bank of Ireland, found asking prices in Dublin rose at an annualised rate of 2.1 per cent in the third quarter while those outside the capital rose at a rate of 4.8 per cent.

The median asking price for newly-listed properties nationally was €390,000 in the third quarter while in Dublin it was €480,000.

There was a modicum of good news for prospective buyers with MyHome noting that homebuilding in Ireland hit a new post-crash record of 38,000 homes built in the year to June, enough to accommodate 100,000 people.

Ireland records one of lowest rates of house price inflation in euro zone

This exceeded population growth, which was 67,000, for the first time in the series.

“This – along with a 12.5 per cent year-on-year increase in homes listed for sale on MyHome – is positive news for homebuyers,” it said.

The number of properties listed for sale on MyHome at end of last month was 14,630. It also noted there have been 10,400 new listings for sale on MyHome since June, which is up 5.3 per cent year-on-year.

However, it predicted that existing home sales was likely to contract for a fourth consecutive quarter.

“The rate of asking price inflation continues to slow, the number of properties for sale on MyHome is rising, and homebuilding has picked up,” Bank of Ireland chief economist Conall MacCoille said.

“All of these factors point to positive news for homebuyers. It still makes more financial sense to buy rather than rent, with rental yields still outpacing mortgage rates,” MacCoille said.

What is behind the slowdown in Ireland’s property prices?

The typical joint income of first-time buyers in 2025 was €95,000, purchasing a property worth €408,000, equivalent to four times’ their income, he said.

MacCoille forecast 39,600 new home completions in 2026, rising to 42,000 in 2027.

“This is still a far better outlook than many commentators had suggested just 12 to 18 months ago,” he said.

The report also included an analysis of the impact of Building Energy Ratings (Ber) on price, compiled in conjunction with the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland.

It showed that the value of a typical home rises by 2.7 per cent for each step on the scale – with maximum increase of 10-13 per cent going from C-rated to A-rated home.

MyHome managing director Joanne Geary said the report represented good news for homebuyers but noted that there was still a wide discrepancy between the first-time buyer and mover markets.

“First-time buyer transactions are up by 12 per cent year-on-year while mover transactions have fallen by 1.2 per cent,” she said.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[In making a mess of the budget, Patrick O’Donovan may have done us a favour]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/10/13/in-making-a-mess-of-the-budget-patrick-odonovan-may-have-done-us-a-favour/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/10/13/in-making-a-mess-of-the-budget-patrick-odonovan-may-have-done-us-a-favour/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000It’s been a turbulent few days for the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, Patrick O’Donovan. It was bad enough that his heavily flagged proposal to introduce a €100 culture card for young people was conspicuous by its absence from last Tuesday’s budget.

Worse was to follow when it emerged, to widespread surprise, that RTÉ would not be receiving the €20 million increase in funding agreed as part of a multiannual restructuring deal in 2024. The surprise seemed to be shared by the Taoiseach and Tánaiste, whose intervention reportedly led to an emergency meeting between the Minister and RTÉ’s chair and director general on Thursday.

While all concerned were tight-lipped afterwards, it has been clearly signalled that the Government will stump up the €20 million, subject to RTÉ satisfying the Minister on the progress of its reform and redundancy programme. Given that these were always the terms on which the multiannual payments were based, there is as yet no clear explanation as to why the money was withheld in the first place.

None of this is good for O’Donovan’s political reputation, and there were mutterings from various unnamed Government figures over the weekend that he might not keep his Cabinet seat when the midterm reshuffle takes place at the end of next year.

The Limerick TD seems to have an unfortunate knack for losing friends and alienating people, but last week’s embarrassments and the subsequent clean-up may have forced the question of how RTÉ is funded back on to the agenda, and that would not be a bad thing.

The current arrangement was agreed by the previous government in the summer of 2024. It guaranteed RTÉ €725 million in public money over three years, rising from €225 million in 2025 to €240 million this year and €260 million in 2027. The licence fee was retained, and the Exchequer committed to making up the difference between what it brought in and the agreed total. The lower amount raised from licence revenue, the bigger the cheque from the State.

That difference is growing quickly. Licence sales have fallen every year since the 2023 payments scandal. Figures released by O’Donovan last week show sales down 6 per cent in the first nine months of this year, putting full-year income on course for about €114 million, compared with more than €150 million in 2022.

Less widely understood is how much of the licence fee the State already pays. The Department of Social Protection funds free licences for everyone over 70 and others who qualify for the household benefits package, a bill in excess of €80 million a year. That is more than 500,000 licences, set against roughly 715,000 bought by households this year.

Free licences grow by up to 20,000 a year as the population ages, while paid ones keep falling. Remarkably, if current trends hold, licences paid for by social protection will outnumber those paid for by households as early as 2029. This seems untenable.

Does Patrick O’Donovan’s explanation for €20m RTÉ funding cut add up?

Add the direct top-up and the picture is starker still. In 2025, about 54 per cent of RTÉ’s public funding came from the Exchequer in one form or another. By 2027, that share is likely to be above 60 per cent. The licence fee survives in name, but the money increasingly comes directly from Government.

European law now has something to say about this. The European Media Freedom Act requires member states to fund public broadcasters through transparent procedures based on objective criteria set in advance, and to ensure they have “adequate, sustainable and predictable” resources. The point is to protect editorial independence by making sure money cannot be used as a political lever. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill now before the Oireachtas is meant to give effect to those rules here.

Last week’s episode looks much more like political incompetence than a deliberate act of interference. But cutting an agreed sum at a few hours’ notice, without explanation, is clearly not in keeping with the spirit of the EU rules. Whatever its cause, it has shown how easily the money can be turned on and off.

Nor should the role of ill-will be underestimated. Members of the Oireachtas media committee have indicated they intend to question RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst about a newspaper column by radio presenter Oliver Callan, which questioned Simon Harris’s credentials as Minister for Finance. One source described Callan’s piece as “antigovernment”. Whether a presenter’s newspaper column should be a matter for a committee examining RTÉ’s finances is debatable. That the two are being raised alongside each other is telling.

The new legislation will strengthen the role of Coimisiún na Meán, which will assess RTÉ’s needs and recommend a level of funding for each three-year period. But the regulator’s role will be advisory. There will be no legal obligation on the minister of the day to follow its recommendations, nor, as far as can be seen, any requirement to explain a decision not to. The final call will remain where it was last week, with a politician putting together a budget.

The licence fee has many faults, including the fact that it is now collapsing before our eyes. But it was based on a sound principle. Money paid directly by citizens to a public service broadcaster, at arm’s length from the government of the day, gave that broadcaster a degree of independence that an annual grant cannot.

If public service broadcasting is to retain public trust and integrity, it must be insulated from political pressure, whether born of malice or just haplessness. If nothing else, we can thank O’Donovan for reminding us of that.

RTÉ funding snub not a good look for Patrick O’Donovan

It comes as Irish household wealth has grown rapidly. In 2023, total net household wealth in Ireland was two and a half times the amount it had been just 10 years earlier, according to the report.

Although the share of that wealth held by the poorest half of households has increased in that time, almost half of all wealth continues to be controlled by the wealthiest 10 per cent of Irish households.

The structure of household wealth has also changed, the report found, with business assets accounting for a larger share “particularly among households at the top of the wealth distribution”. Further down the wealth chain, the family home continues to account for the largest share of household wealth.

The study found that, to maximise revenue, all assets outside pension funds should be taxed, with no exemptions for things like family homes, farms or businesses.

“Our wealth tax scenario analysis shows that the breadth of the tax base matters more for revenue potential than the threshold at which liability begins, with broad-base scenarios consistently generating larger aggregate tax liabilities than those with extensive exemptions,” write authors Rachel Slaymaker and Chi Tran of the ESRI and Department of Finance economists Federica De Blasio and Emmet Ryan.

Doing so, the research paper showed, would allow the tax to be set above a very high threshold where only the richest 1.5 per cent of Irish households would be affected.

It accepted that including business wealth, farms and the family home would be politically sensitive. As they are less liquid, such assets would also be harder to value on an ongoing basis.

Tax-rich Ireland at one remove from debt zeitgeist

If you allow fairly wide exemptions, the paper argued, you need to dramatically lower the threshold, bringing many more households into the wealth tax net to secure reasonable tax revenue.

The report cited the 2022 Commission on Taxation and Welfare recommendation for a gradual shift from taxing work towards taxes on wealth, capital, property and consumption, to meet the increased costs of an ageing population, public services and the climate transition, “while maintaining fiscal sustainability”.

However, it accepted that, all households, even the wealthiest could have trouble finding the cash to meet wealth tax liabilities from cash income.

Wealth taxes fell from favour in the early years of the century, the report said. Twelve European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 but by this year, only Norway, Spain and Switzerland do so.

Limited yields, administrative and valuation difficulties, avoidance and evasion, were cited as reasons for the tax’s diminishing popularity, alongside concerns of governments around capital mobility.

Concerns around the concentration of wealth, together with pressures on public finances and the limitations of tax systems that rely predominantly on income flows, have contributed to renewed international interest in net wealth taxation in recent years.

“Recent research has increasingly emphasised that the effects of a wealth tax depend not only on whether wealth is taxed, but on how such taxes are designed,” the report said.

Getting your head around childcare costs can be fiendishly complex. There are different subsidies depending on your financial status and the age of the child and different bands depending on how long the child is in care.

And if it is any consolation, it is not just you and other parents who get confused. In his speech, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Jack Chambers, did say he was “reducing the maximum childcare fees paid by parents, from €735 to €550 per month for children up to senior infants”, putting €2,200 a year back into parents’ pockets.

Not quite – at least not for everyone, including you. But that does not mean there was not good news for you on childcare in the budget – at least from September of next year when the budget childcare measures kick in.

The Minister was referring to the maximum amount a parent of a child receiving between 40 and 50 hours of care a week can be charged in a creche that has signed up to the Government’s “core funding” scheme, where Government subsidises the cost of care. This is called Band E.

If you are paying €1,000 – or more accurately €959 – a month, you will be in Band F, where your child is receiving care for more than 50 hours a week.

And you are far from alone in having been taken aback by talk of the €735 and €550 maximums.

The Minister’s team insist that Band E is the one most commonly used by parents across the State. That may be so; the statement was not accompanied by figures. The net cost to you is determined by two things: fee per band and the personal subsidy to which each child is entitled, depending on your income.

Under the budget measures, the fee for Band F will fall from €336 a week to €300. And, for those on the universal subsidy (anyone with family income of more than €73,000), the subsidy for children up to senior infants will rise to €2.50 from €2.15 per hour up to a maximum of 45 hours.

If your income is below €73,000, the subsidy may be higher and, if it is below €36,500, that could be as high as €5.10 an hour.

When they say household income, they mean income minus any pension contributions you pay. You also do not include certain welfare payments and, if you have more than one child, there are further income disregards.

Anyway, back to the numbers. That €2.50 an hour universal subsidy amounts to €112.50 a week. Taking this from your €300 “fee”, you are left with €187.50. From September next year (11 months in the future), that will be your weekly fee, amounting to €750 a month.

That means a fall of at least €209 in your childcare cost per child each month, or somewhere between €2,300 and €2,500 over the year. So good news, if not quite a drop in charge to €550.

We should learn more about the new product when the Finance Bill is published later this week, but, given that we already have tax free savings products through the State Savings scheme, it’s likely that the new products will be most attractive to those who are willing to take on some element of risk for a greater return.

The young investor

Anyone can open an account once they are 18 and have a PPS number. And, as no minimum investment applies, it’s expected that you’ll be able to start investing from as little as €20 or so, though the product providers that will launch products next year may impose their own minimums.

In the UK, for example, some ISA providers allow you to invest as little as £1 a month, although many do apply minimums of £50-£100.

Young investors could look to the new product to build up their knowledge of investing; to save for big future purchases such as a house (especially if this is at least five years or more away); or for a rainy day or trip around the world.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work

Saving €50 a month, for example, will give a return of about €1,291 after two years, based on an annual return of 7 per cent. But keep investing for longer, and you could have €8,704 after 10 years, or more than €26,000 after 20.

If you hadn’t started the account, saving €50 a month in your current account would give just €12,000 after 20 years. The potential upside is clear, although you do need to bear in mind that markets can fall as well as rise, so there is a risk. And product provider charges, which will only become clear next July, will reduce these gains.

And what about tax? Well, in a PIA your investment can grow tax free for quite a long time if you’re only investing small amounts. This is a significant advantage. As a comparison, if you held your money outside a PIA, and cashed your savings in after 10 years, you would pay tax on your “profit” of €2,704. Based on the current exit tax rate of 35 per cent, that could cost you almost €1,000 to Revenue.

Annual management charge 0.07 per cent

These funds aim to diversify your investment across a range of products – such as cash, bonds, equities and property – and smooth returns through volatile stages of the markets. However, they may have higher charges than some competing funds.

But again, investing and holding for the long term can deliver strong returns.

Someone investing €200 a month, for example, with an average annual return of 4 per cent, would have a fund worth about €5,000 after two years, almost €30,000 after 10 years and close to €75,000 after 20 years.

Possible tax bill This saver could hit the €50,000 mark after about 15 years (although that limit could have increased by then). So a possible bill of about €38.46 a year, based on assets of €53,846.

Product provider charges Unknown

Annual management charge 0.9 per cent

The lump-sum investor

If you’re one of the people with a share of the €170 billion on deposit in Irish banks, earning a negligible return, you might want to transfer some of your savings directly into the new product.

While the full details of the new product have yet to emerge, it’s expected that you will be able to fund your new PIA with a lump sum, up to the annual limit.

This means you could seed your new PIA with a €12,000 lump sum, and so could your spouse (so €24,000 per couple), with lump sums made every year thereafter. On this basis, tax would kick in from year five or so.

If it’s in a savings account, you’ll be paying Dirt each year, at a rate of 33 per cent, capital gains tax at 31 per cent if it’s directly invested in shares, or exit tax at 35 per cent if moving out of a fund (provided you encash after January 1st).

Possible tax bill €0 until the fund reaches €50,000

Product provider charges Unknown

Annual management charge 0.2 per cent

The unlucky investor

Not everything must go up. And if you need to cash in your money when markets are down, you face the risk of losing your money.

As our example shows, if you invest €500 a month over 10 years, but your average return is minus-1 per cent, you will end up losing almost €3,000. And, as you have tipped over the €50,000 mark, you will also have a tax bill – even though you have been losing money.

]]>Orla Murray/Coalesce<![CDATA[Frantic behind-the-scenes talks delivers deal on EU capital markets reform]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/frantic-behind-the-scenes-talks-delivers-deal-on-eu-capital-markets-reform/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/frantic-behind-the-scenes-talks-delivers-deal-on-eu-capital-markets-reform/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000When the EU’s finance ministers sat down for a working dinner in Luxembourg last Thursday evening, Simon Harris warned his counterparts they could be about to face another day of newspaper headlines bashing Europe for again ducking a big decision.

We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years

]]>AILBE PHOTO<![CDATA[Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/12/budget-reversal-of-the-policy-on-tackling-climate-change-was-a-mistake/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/12/budget-reversal-of-the-policy-on-tackling-climate-change-was-a-mistake/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000There are three crucial tasks for any budget: does it implement a long-term economic strategy; is the trajectory of the public finances sustainable; and will it manage aggregate demand in the economy so that economic activity remains close to capacity?

This year the strategic priorities for the Government should be to enhance the economic security of the State and promote long-term growth, tackle climate change, and reduce poverty, especially child poverty.

The budget has further increased our dependence on corporation tax as indirect taxes are reduced, increasing the economy’s vulnerability. However, unlike many other economies, we will still run a small surplus next year; it is just that it should be much larger.

This budget scores well on growth, committing increased resources for infrastructural investment. Government investment, which is €20 billion this year, will increase by almost 15 per cent in 2027. This is more than 5 per cent of national income, much higher than in other countries, reflecting our rapid population growth.

Some of this investment will go on the start-up of MetroLink and other projects, but the fruits of this investment will only be fully apparent many elections hence. Jam today would have been easier for the Government, but this is the right answer.

Where the budget is faulty is the reversal of the policy on tackling climate change. The carbon tax was due to rise gradually to 2030 to encourage us to reduce emissions and to fund investment in key climate projects, such as retrofitting and protecting those on low incomes. This budget has reversed this, cutting the tax rate on certain fuels, with a commitment to leave it at this low level to 2030. This sends all the wrong signals, and it also means there will be significantly fewer resources to protect those who are energy poor and to fund important climate investment, including flood protection.

The number of children in poverty is increasing, despite our run of economic success. Research by the ESRI has shown that the best way to tackle this problem would be to introduce targeted income supports for children living in low-income families. An opportunity to do this was missed last week.

Dealing with the effects of higher inflation on living standards is best done in a number of ways. The income tax system should be indexed so that the tax take does not increase by stealth. In contrast to last year, this budget does this.

The exceptionally high energy prices pose particular problems for those on low incomes, with higher expenditure on heating. This clearly needed to be addressed, and the best way of doing it would have been to increase welfare payments and introduce targeted support for the energy needs of the most vulnerable.

The Government won’t raise carbon tax again but promises to decarbonise the economy – how?

Instead, Government expenditure on social payments will rise by only 2.7 per cent next year, less than inflation, and there is no significant targeted support for those who need it most.

More of the reduction in excise tax on fuel goes to those on high incomes, reducing the incentive to cut our emissions of greenhouse gases. None of it goes to those who cannot afford a car. An unsatisfactory outcome for the climate, and for those on low incomes who will suffer from the cold this winter.

If the Government sticks to the numbers in the budget it looks likely that it will be neutral, neither stimulating nor deflating the economy. While some tightening would have been better, the stimulus largely arises from the very desirable increase in public investment.

The budgetary numbers published last week also show the share of public expenditure in national income next year will remain roughly unchanged compared to this year. If this proves to be the outcome, it would be satisfactory. However, as with recent budgets, this one carries the seeds of another overrun.

It is no surprise that Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers did not put a precise number on the provision for public service pay next year. He is beginning a negotiating process, and anything he provided would be taken just as the starting point by trade unions. Thus, there is likely to be some overrun to provide for the final outturn of the pay talks.

The provision for social payments looks like an underestimate of what will be spent. Also, once again in some departmental budgets, it looks as if the estimates do not provide for expenditure that will prove unavoidable, for example in health.

While on paper the budget numbers look moderately prudent, as in previous years, they may prove a poor guide to the eventual outturn.

]]>Paul Faith<![CDATA[More needs to be done to help home-grown companies scale and offset reliance on FDI]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/more-needs-to-be-done-to-help-home-grown-companies-scale-and-offset-reliance-on-fdi/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/more-needs-to-be-done-to-help-home-grown-companies-scale-and-offset-reliance-on-fdi/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 04:31:00 +0000Ireland’s economic model has been one of the great success stories of modern Europe. Our multinational sector has transformed employment and public finances. But we have come to a point now when what made us stand apart feels a little less different and we need to look at future-proofing our economy.

At the same time, Ireland’s private sector continues to underperform when it comes to scaling indigenous companies into globally competitive multinationals. Ireland needs to enhance its offering to FDI as well as putting measures in place to help its home-grown businesses scale into global companies.

Ireland’s corporation tax receipts rose from €4.7 billion in 2014 to €32.9 billion in 2025, now accounting for about 31 per cent of total exchequer tax revenue, compared with just 8.3 per cent in 2014.

This concentration is more than 2.5 times the OECD average (12 per cent). Revenue analysis shows that foreign-owned multinationals generate almost 90 per cent of these receipts, while the three largest companies accounted for 46 per cent of all corporation tax paid in 2024.

While it is unlikely that there will be a significant reduction in corporation tax receipts over the next few years, the picture is far less certain over a 10- to 15-year horizon. The challenge for policymakers is that decisions about future investment are being made today. If Ireland waits until corporation tax receipts begin to decline before responding, it may be too late to attract the next wave of investment required to sustain our spending commitments and economic success. The Government needs to act now.

There are several ways Ireland can enhance its offering to international companies as well as doing more for home-grown private businesses.

Firstly, Ireland needs to invest now for the future. This is not simply about protecting existing industries; it is about identifying the sectors that will drive economic growth in the decades ahead and putting the policies, infrastructure and incentives in place now to attract them.

Ireland should be reinvesting part of today’s corporation tax revenues to develop domestic businesses, support innovation and secure the next generation of FDI. The objective should be clear: act while the tide is still coming in, not after it has turned.

Secondly, Ireland needs to become a more compelling location for high-value research, development and innovation activities. The current R&D tax credit, despite small enhancements in Budget 2027, would benefit from expanding the range of activities covered.

State’s tax take boosted by €3bn as multinationals ‘front-load’ payments

The relief should be expanded to increase the benefit for advanced manufacturing investment opportunities. Budget 2027 missed an opportunity to introduce a separate innovation incentive for broader innovation activities, supporting investment in areas such as digitalisation and decarbonisation. These reforms would strengthen Ireland’s attractiveness as a global innovation hub while further supporting private companies.

Thirdly, too many promising private businesses are acquired before they reach scale. Irish firms face systemic barriers that limit their ability to grow and scale. Three things are needed to help – capital, capabilities and culture.

The Government has begun to recognise the capital challenge through its proposed €1 billion Scaling Fund announced in Budget 2027. This is a welcome start, but much will depend on the accessibility of funds. Scaling an Irish business towards a public listing should be more attractive and achievable – Euronext Dublin has only about two dozen actively traded equities, compared with nearly 2,000 listed companies across European markets.

The introduction of the State investment account is also a welcome step towards mobilising pools of capital in Ireland, with the potential to channel significant household savings towards active investment and broaden participation in capital markets. The next challenge is ensuring that a meaningful proportion of those funds is channelled into promising Irish companies, helping to create the next generation of indigenous businesses.

While the budget announcement to reduce Capital Gains Tax to 31 per cent is positive, a larger reduction to 20 per cent would have gone a lot further towards encouraging further investment. Furthermore, revised entrepreneur relief should be enhanced and retirement relief expanded.

Irish businesses need the talent, leadership and expertise to help them scale from successful start-ups into global enterprises. The announcement of funding to the National Training Fund to build skills and resilience fit for an AI-enabled workforce was a practical step and a sign that the State can provide supports to nurture these capabilities. But more of this is needed. Finally, Ireland must create a culture that rewards ambition, celebrates success and makes scaling indigenous businesses a national priority.

Budget 2027: Measures put public finances on worse trajectory, State watchdog warns

Not every competitiveness issue requires money. Often, smaller businesses face administration burdens that consume valuable time and resources without delivering meaningful economic benefits. Simplification has minimal cost to the exchequer but can have a significant impact.

For example, in our pre-budget submission, we suggested pre-populated simplified tax returns for small businesses. The budget move to allow enhanced reporting requirements to be submitted monthly rather than on a real-time basis is a welcome step. Ireland does not need a completely new economic model. The foundations of our success remain strong. However, maintaining success in a changing world requires enhancing our offering to FDI and the private sector – reinvesting for competitiveness. The real question is whether we are prepared to invest today in what will make us attractive tomorrow.

Paraic Burke is head of tax at PwC Ireland
