]]>MilosStankovic<![CDATA[Ireland goes Swedish on investment, but deemed disposal remains a problem]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 03:01:00 +0000Earlier this year, Stocktake suggested Minister for Finance Simon Harris might be tempted to borrow Sweden’s model for encouraging people to invest.

It turns out he was. The Savings and Investment Account (SIA) announced in Budget 2027 is not a carbon copy of Sweden’s ISK, but the resemblance is clear.

Investors can put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with the first €50,000 of investments exempt from tax, while amounts above that will face an annual 1 per cent charge.

Some will be irked by that charge, especially in years where stock markets have fallen. However, a UK-style tax-free wrapper, allowing savers to invest up to £20,000 a year completely free of tax, always appeared excessively generous and politically indefensible.

For the Government, a Swedish-type approach offers a predictable tax stream while encouraging people to put their savings into shares and funds (and a €50,000 tax-free limit is more generous than many expected) rather than leaving them in cash.

However, the new account also highlights the problem with the system outside it. Investments held in the SIA will escape deemed disposal, while investors buying ordinary ETFs will continue to face an eight-year tax charge on unrealised gains, albeit at the reduced rate of 35 per cent.

The Government says it intends to move beyond deemed disposal during the lifetime of this administration, but substantive reform has again been deferred.

And there is a second, less discussed problem. The Funds Sector 2030 review recommended limited loss relief, but the Government’s roadmap says it will not be introduced. As Stocktake previously noted, an investor who makes €5,000 on one ETF and loses €5,000 on another can therefore have no overall gain but still face tax on the €5,000 profit.

Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?

That is less of an issue for someone holding one broad global ETF, but it matters for a portfolio of separate funds.

Some will have issues with the SIA, but it’s arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler. The harder task is making the wider investing tax system equally sensible.

]]>Nick Bradshaw / The Irish Times<![CDATA[‘Nobody wants to work’: Why doesn’t Ireland grow more veg?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/environment/2026/10/10/why-doesnt-ireland-grow-more-veg/https://www.irishtimes.com/environment/2026/10/10/why-doesnt-ireland-grow-more-veg/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000“Nobody wants to work,” Jenny McNally laughs when asked what might turn someone away from a career in vegetable growing.

“It’s hard labour; your bones ache. There’s nothing easy about horticultural farming.”

Since 1997, she and her husband Patrick have operated an organic, family farm in north Co Dublin, selling their produce directly at markets and from a shop on-site. On the couple’s 99 acres, they cultivate a wide variety of vegetables, salad and some fruit.

At one point during the 1990s, there were more than 600 commercial vegetable growers in Ireland. Today, there are fewer than 70.

A recent report by the Climate Change Advisory Council noted that an estimated 83 per cent of fruit and vegetables consumed in the Republic are imported from overseas.

“When you hear about another veg producer going out of business, sometimes it’s because there’s nobody there following behind,” McNally says.

“There are no children, or the farmer’s children are not interested. They’ve seen mum and dad work so hard all their life and why should they do it?”

Fortunately, three of the five McNally children are part of the family business. If it weren’t for their involvement, “Pat and myself would be growing a tunnel of salads or something and that would be it,” McNally says.

Before 1997, they had been conventional farmers, raising livestock and growing barley and oats as well as vegetables.

People like us, we had moved into growing courgettes and beans and mangetout

Jenny McNally

From a commercial point of view, McNally says that there was no security around veg in the open market. You were “always on a wing and a prayer”, and never guaranteed a sale.

That culture made life difficult for smaller farms, and it was compounded by a growing need for expensive equipment and machinery.

McNally says that over time, a lot of sellers were pushed out. It suited supermarkets to work with larger, specialised operations focusing on large-scale production of individual vegetables.

“People like us, we had moved into growing courgettes and beans and mangetout,” McNally says.

“We were told if you don’t have a refrigerated van and a cold store, you’re not up to our expectations and our levels, so that was that. At the time, we had five small children and there was no way we could afford to even think of anything like that.”

The solution was a stall at Temple Bar Food Market where they could sell “wonky courgettes”, beans that weren’t topped and tailed, and “cabbages that weren’t all exactly the same size”. It turned out a market for this sort of food existed.

McNally Family Farm veg can be bought at three markets today. Queues often form before they have had a chance to lay out their produce. They have built up relationships with their customers over three decades, many of whom have grown to appreciate the journey from farm to fork, are understanding of seasonal setbacks that impact the size or volume of what’s being sold.

This summer of 2026 – Ireland’s hottest on record – was difficult for vegetable producers.

A recent report carried out by Teagasc, the national agriculture and food development authority, found that in 2026, there were yield and quality losses of 25 to 40 per cent on unirrigated vegetable crops.

Irrigated fields were protected, albeit at a price. For some crops, growers spent more than €2,700 per hectare on water alone, before equipment and infrastructure costs.

Only 30 to 35 per cent of the Irish vegetable production area carries sufficient irrigation capacity.

“Ultimately, it’s an increased cost of production,” says Dermot Callaghan, head of horticulture at Teagasc.

“Irrigation costs money to do, between ‘cap-ex’ and ‘op-ex’ – so, capital expenditure on the equipment and infrastructure, including reservoirs which may be needed in the future, and operational costs, the ‘op-ex’, which is the cost of actually moving irrigation systems, pumping stations, running diesel pumps to extract water and so on.”

The positive, he explains, is that Ireland has something of an advantage on its European neighbours when it comes to accessing water.

Though investment will be needed for farmers to adapt to the effects of the climate crisis over the coming years, it should be cheaper to irrigate here than in hotter countries.

Over the last few years, Teagasc has carried out a series of cost studies on horticulture farms, documenting a trend of rising costs that has not been matched by the farm gate price – in other words, the value of the farmer’s produce as it leaves the farm.

According to the agriculture and food authority’s most recent report, labour accounts for 43.4 per cent of costs on horticulture farms.

It is a figure that echoes Jenny McNally’s concerns around the availability of labour in horticulture. Callaghan says the answer, where possible, is to adopt technology, automation and even robotics.

Ireland could be growing huge quantities of fruit and vegetables

James O’Donovan, Vegan Society of Ireland

“Still, there are crops which have to be touched by the human hand,”says Callaghan, “and those are the crops which will obviously have a higher labour cost associated [with them], and will probably be the last to get automated. Having labour to do that job will be paramount.”

Six supermarkets signed up to a “horticulture grower-retail charter” this year, establishing five ‘key principles’ intended to support a stronger and more sustainable sector.

The charter commits to improved communication and promotion around Irish produce, as well as a sustainable approach to cost inputs and reduced food waste.

“They’re prepared now to work on a longer, three- to five-year arrangement with growers, which is a big change because that will allow growers to invest in their businesses,” Callaghan says.

“They have a line of sight on having a market for their product.”

Efforts are being made to encourage more domestic growers. Over the last couple of years, the Department of Agriculture’s Organic Farming Scheme (OFS) was opened up to horticultural producers.

Recently, the scheme helped fund the digging of a new well on the McNally family farm.

More than 250 commercial growers across fruit, vegetable and potato sectors are operating under Bord Bia’s Sustainable Horticulture Assurance Scheme (SHAS), generating a farm gate value of about €652 million in 2025.

Emer Gallahar Hall, the senior manager for horticulture at Bord Bia, says the drop in the number of individual vegetable growers in Ireland since the 1990s “should not be interpreted as a proportional decline in output”, but rather a reflection of the reality that vegetable production is “increasingly concentrated among fewer, larger, highly specialised businesses”.

Ireland is a “net importer of fresh produce,” Gallahar Hall says, though a substantial portion of imported fruit and vegetables, such as citrus fruits, bananas and Mediterranean crops, cannot be commercially produced in Ireland due to the Irish climate.

Bord Bia recently launched HortLink, a community network for growers and professionals in horticulture to come together and share their experiences.

It ties into another concern Jenny McNally raises: that sometimes the most important thing “is to be able to chat to other farmers”.

Despite the various ongoing initiatives, Gallahar Hall notes that economic viability remains a key challenge in horticulture, with growers facing an increase of 51 per cent in production costs since 2021.

The Vegan Society of Ireland suggests looking abroad. In October 2023, Denmark launched a world-first, plant-based action plan designed to increase the number of vegetarian foods in the national diet and reduce the climate footprint of its agricultural industry.

Backed by a €170 million government fund, it targets a full suite of improvements to the Danish domestic food chain, from farms and food processors to retail and restaurants. In advance of Budget 2027, the vegan society called on the Irish Government to introduce a similar programme.

“[Ireland and Denmark are] super similar,” says the society’s chairperson James O’Donovan on the potential for the agricultural sector.

“Ireland could be growing huge quantities of fruit and vegetables.”

O’Donovan suggests that less food could be imported across the board. Sugar and bread, he says, have potential to become stronger domestic products.

The vegan society advocates for a move towards organic foods – a transition that is also prioritised by Denmark’s action plan.

In May, the society commissioned a survey to gauge the Irish public’s attitude to plant-based foods. Four in five respondents said they wanted to eat more fruit, vegetables and legumes, while 62 per cent said Ireland should make healthy, sustainable diets a national political priority. O’Donovan sees this as a “clear mandate” for politicians to act.

“The quantity of fruits and vegetables that we’re importing is huge,” he says.

“The quantity of legumes and grains and tillage crops that we’re importing is also huge. That’s why we’re calling for a holistic approach – just increasing Ireland’s food security.”

]]><![CDATA[‘Can we cancel our Help to Buy application and apply for the updated amount?’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/11/help-to-buy-applicants-worry-they-could-miss-out-on-5000-budget-uplift/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/11/help-to-buy-applicants-worry-they-could-miss-out-on-5000-budget-uplift/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 10:36:07 +0000With regards to the increase in the Help to Buy, we have signed contracts in recent weeks and are availing of the Help to Buy to make up part of our deposit.

We have not yet drawn it down as we are awaiting signed contracts from the builders’ solicitors. Can we cancel our current help to buy application and apply for the updated amount? What is the risk in doing so?

Our solicitors don’t know the answer and we are awaiting a response from Revenue also.

We are very conscious this matter is time sensitive, as payment of our deposit is required in the coming weeks.

AT

You are just one of several first-time buyers who was in touch with us after the Minister announced an expansion of the relief available under Help-to-Buy. Purchasing a first home is always a mix of the exciting and the terrifying and the process is complex enough without last minute changes to the rules.

In a budget where pretty much everything was leaked in advance, the decision to increase the amount of tax relief available for Help to Buy applicants was not something people saw coming.

In fact, if there was to be reform of the system, it was expected it would address the reality for many looking to buy in or close to Dublin and other big urban centres – that the €500,000 cap on the value of property purchases under the scheme locks out many aspiring first-time buyers.

As one reader put it: “The scheme remains redundant to majority of buyers in Dublin, commuter towns and other cities across the country. The extra €5k does not unlock any new homes or help affordability.” Of course, that was what it was intended to do in the first place.

There is certainly a broader policy debate on whether housing incentive schemes, such as Help to Buy, which were always designed to help developers as much or more than buyers, are an effective use of government funds to ease a housing crisis but we’ll not get into that here.

Your concerns are much more practical. You are in the process and, clearly, this extra €5,000 would be beneficial to you if you are able to claim it.

So what happens to applications that are “in the system”? Do they get assessed under the new rules? Can they be withdrawn and a new application made? And what effect, if any, might that have on your home purchase?

You are not alone. Aideen was also in touch with our Q&A, wanting to know whether she would need to reapply given they have not closed on their home.

And Michelle, who is using the relief, to build her own home and has been approved for the “old” €30,000 relief but has not yet claimed the money has much the same query.

Mairéad is further along in the process, having already received €30,000 under the scheme. Is she now entitled to this additional €5,000 in relief, she wonders.

For Mairéad, the answer, unsurprisingly, is “no”. If you have already got your money, as with any other tax and relief headings, your application was assessed under rules in place at the time and you cannot benefit (or suffer) from changes in the rules subsequent to receiving your benefit.

Revenue confirmed for me that the new rules kick in on October 7th, the day after the budget. That follows the passing of financial resolution on the budget change to the scheme in the Oireachtas.

Who is eligible? Anyone who has either not signed a contract to buy their home before October 7th or, in the case of those building their own homes, has not yet drawn down the first tranche of their approved mortgage loan.

Revenue notes that some taxpayers may have submitted an application to see if they are eligible or to find out the amount they are eligible to claim under Help to Buy.

“The test to be applied, however, is whether they have signed a contract to purchase a qualifying property or made the first draw down of a mortgage (in the case of a self-build qualifying property),” they tell me.

Minister rules out raising cap on Help-to-Buy scheme for homes worth over €500k

So if you signed the contract with the developer to buy your home before last Wednesday (October 7th) or, for self-build projects, had drawn down any of your mortgage before that date, you will not benefit from the new, higher tax relief threshold.

In your case, although you have not yet drawn down any funds under the relief, you say you have signed the contracts – albeit you are waiting for them to come back from the builder’s side, so it appears you will not benefit from the budget measure and will be able to draw down a maximum of €30,000 in tax relief, not €35,000.

Aideen, who says she has not closed on her home, may be eligible as long as she has not signed the purchase contract. Similarly, Michelle, who is building her own place – or having it built for her – may be eligible if she has not drawn down any of her mortgage.

In her case, it does not matter whether she has actually taken ownership of the Help to Buy relief but whether she has tapped her mortgage on the property.

In those cases, where approval had been granted but not activated by any contract or draw down, I expect you will certainly have to reapply as Revenue will have completed the application paperwork.

What is not so clear is what happens for people who have applied to the scheme but have yet to receive Revenue confirmation that they have been accepted. It would make sense that Revenue would apply the new limits to cases in the system but they have not yet confirmed that for me.

Risk

You do raise an interesting related point which, though it appears is not relevant for you at this point, might be for others earlier in the process who are considering reapplying for the scheme to benefit under new rules – what is the risk in doing so?

With demand still exceeding supply, there is always a danger that any delay in the process could see the other side move on to another buyer.

If contracts are in place, everyone is bound by them – and you lose out on the €5,000 – but if there are no contracts yet in place, there is nothing to stop the developer moving on to another buyer rather than waiting for someone to reapply for Help to Buy under new rules – or raise the price of the property.

That’s not to say they will but there is certainly a risk that they might.

Scheme rules

For those looking to apply now for Help to Buy, what do the changes mean.

Essentially, Help to Buy allows you to claim back income tax and deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) you have paid over the four tax years before the one in which you are making the application to help pull together the deposit you need to buy your first home.

All parties to the purchase must be first time buyers and the property must be newly-build, not second-hand. The property cannot be valued at anything above €500,000 and you must also be taking out a mortgage that covers at least 70 per cent of the price of the property.

The maximum you can claim under the new rules is €35,000 or 10 per cent of the property price, whichever is the lower. Before the budget, the figure was €30,000; all other Ts & Cs were the same.

That €35,000 is the relief that applies to the property, not to the individual, so if two of you are buying, you cannot double up the relief to secure €70,000.

The contractor or developer selling you the property must also be on an approved Revenue list which you can find here. That means they have registered under the scheme and, more important from the Revenue perspective, are compliant with taxes.

To be fair, it would be exceptionally unusual for a developer building new homes not to be on the list but it is always worth checking.

Finally, if you do not live in the property for at least five years, you will face a clawback from Revenue of some of the relief granted.

The scheme has been extended – both in scope and deadline – several times since it was first introduced in 2016. As of now, it is scheduled to run until December 31st, 2029.

]]><![CDATA[A good night’s sleep is a class issue]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000In the 1920s, a pair of sociologists set out to study “the interwoven trends that are the life of a small American city” at a time of rapid change.

In their subsequent book about Muncie, Indiana (which they anonymised as “Middletown”), they wrote that the community was divided by time as well as class.

At 6am, the lights were going on in working-class households because their jobs generally began between 6.15 and 7.30am (when they weren’t on night shifts), while the “business class” households remained slumbering until later.

These different working rhythms became political in 1925 when a deadlock emerged over whether the city should adopt “daylight saving time”, which would mean longer light on summer evenings.

The working-class early risers argued they would lose sleep, while the businessmen urged the change “because of golf” and the need to deal with businesses on the east coast.

The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. But scientists have learned a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.

In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

It is a myth that night-shift workers can become nocturnal over time. According to the book Life Time by professor of circadian neuroscience Russell Foster, studies suggest that 97 per cent of night shift workers remain synchronised to daytime, which means they have to sleep when their bodies are primed to be awake, and vice versa.

There are consequences for blood pressure and the immune system. The correlations with cancer are so clear that night work has been classed as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer.

Maynooth-led sleep research will examine links with mental health

Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-40s.

Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

But while the prevalence of night work has declined gradually in the US since Middletown was written, there is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock. According to research published this year, most US night workers have no more than a high-school education.

More broadly, the pandemic-induced shift towards remote work has been a bigger boon for white-collar workers (who already had more flexibility over their hours) than anyone else.

What ‘smart’ watches get wrong and right when tracking the quality of your sleep

In Europe, for example, managers have the highest levels of autonomy according to 2024’s vast European Working Conditions Survey, with 40 per cent able to adapt their working hours within certain limits, and 19 per cent having full control over their schedules. In contrast, workers at the bottom end of the pay scale continue to have little control: nearly 80 per cent have schedules set entirely by their employers.

It is possible that advances in automation will eventually do away with the need for humans to work against their body clocks. Already, some logistics companies are beginning to experiment with “lights-out night shifts” in which robots work overnight alone, setting aside those orders that require human assistance until the morning shift arrives.

Self-driving trucks, meanwhile, could cover long highway stretches overnight, saving the “final mile deliveries” for human drivers to do in daytime.

Such a transition would be economically challenging for workers – not least since night-shift work usually pays a premium – but could have huge benefits for human health. It would require careful navigation by policymakers with an eye on science, inequality and the future.

Yet US president Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444906/">
   <title>Öl und KI bestimmen Weltwirtschaft</title>
   <description>Der Internationale Währungsfonds (IWF) rechnet erst nächstes Jahr mit einem stärkeren Wachstum der Weltwirtschaft. Allerdings sei der Ausblick „zweigeteilt“, wie die Organisation am Dienstag in Bangkok mitteilte. Die Industrieländer hätten sich angesichts der seit dem Iran-Krieg gestiegenen Energiepreise widerstandsfähig gezeigt. Sie hätten auch von steigenden Investitionen in künstliche Intelligenz (KI) profitiert. Ärmere Länder, die aus diesem Boom keinen Nutzen zögen, stünden angesichts der Energiepreise vor schweren Entscheidungen.</description>

   <title>Musk will Republikanern Midterms retten</title>
   <description>Wie bei jeglichen Wahlen in den USA spielt Geld auch bei den Midterms in gut drei Wochen eine sehr wichtige Rolle. Vor allem die Republikaner von US-Präsident Donald Trump kämpfen mit hohen Geldsummen gegen schlechte Umfragewerte. Für Aufsehen sorgt nun der Milliardär Elon Musk. Wie die „New York Times“ („NYT“) am Montag berichtete, soll er seit Anfang Juli mehr als 276 Mio. Dollar (247 Mio. Euro) in den Wahlkampf der Republikaner investiert haben.</description>

   <description>In Frankreich sind am Montag mehrere große Supermarktketten Opfer eines Cyberangriffs geworden. Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons.

Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024.

Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga.

W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq

— TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026

According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks.

The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life.

Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services.

However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement.

Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack.

 

Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison.

Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw.

Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years.

Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted.

Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism.

That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025

In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory.

A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe.

Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland.

Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region.

]]> Israeli producer had access to data harvested by Poland using Pegasus spyware, say prosecutors https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/12/israeli-producer-had-access-to-data-harvested-by-poland-using-pegasus-spyware-say-prosecutors/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 12:27:25 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105380

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola…

Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

The former deputy head of Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau has been charged with unlawfully sharing material obtained through surveillance using Pegasus spyware, including communication involving PM @donaldtusk's daughter when Tusk was in opposition https://t.co/LyTuqbq0KQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2025

In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”.

The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister.

“They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.”

Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government.

The pair, who deny wrongdoing, could be jailed for up to three years if found guilty of unlawfully allowing use of the spyware https://t.co/TWjQR74IYT

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026

Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings.

In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information.

The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF.

💬 Jest to dokument o tym, jak władza publiczna w Polsce sięgnęła po narzędzie ingerujące w prawa obywatelskie – powiedziała przewodnicząca komisji śledczej ds. inwigilacji systemem Pegasus @MagdalenaSroka, prezentując raport z prac komisji.https://t.co/MzA9gj4M0Y

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 12, 2026

Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings.

Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family.

Last year, a former deputy justice minister from the PiS government, Michał Woś, was indicted to stand trial over his role in the alleged illegal use of justice ministry funds to help the CBA purchase Pegasus.

]]> US wants Poland to join G20 “as soon as possible” https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/12/us-wants-poland-to-join-g20-as-soon-as-possible/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 11:45:34 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105375

The United States wants Poland to join the G20 “as soon as possible” and intends to raise the issue with other members of the international forum at its forthcoming summit in December in Miami, the US State Department has told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Having previously endorsed Polish membership of the G20 in May, the US now says it intends to “continue discussions with G20 members this year on making Poland a full member as soon as possible”.

“Poland’s long-term and steady economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant,” the State Department told PAP.

Stany Zjednoczone oficjalnie zadeklarowały, że będą zabiegać o stałe członkostwo Polski w G20 https://t.co/lnZ583HIus

— Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) October 11, 2026

The G20, a major intergovernmental forum that brings together 19 major countries together with the European Union and the African Union, is set to meet at a golf resort owned by President Donald Trump in Miami on 14-15 December. Poland is also participating this year as a guest of the United States.

PAP reports that the US has proposed that one of the points in the final declaration adopted by leaders at the conclusion of the summit refer to Poland’s permanent membership. However, this would require the assent of all current members, including Russia.

The issue is likely to be discussed in a pre-summit online meeting of so-called “sherpas” negotiating the text of the declaration, reports PAP.

 

After visiting Washington earlier this month, Marcin Przydacz, the head of President Karol Nawrocki’s international policy office, said that joining the G20 permanently is “Plan A”, but acknowledged that receiving a consensus from existing member states made this variant difficult.

He added that Nawrocki would travel to London before the summit to discuss the possibility of continuing Poland’s guest status next year, when the UK will host the G20. At a meeting of G20 trade ministers last week, finance minister Andrzej Domański said that Poland has a good chance of being invited next year.

Nawrocki also plans to visit G20 members Saudi Arabia and Argentina to canvass for support for Poland’s membership bid, Przydacz has confirmed.

A third option would be for Poland to become a “permanent guest”, a status typically reserved for organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, but also held by Spain.

The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026

Poland has long lobbied for membership in the group. In 2010, then-President Lech Kaczyński said “the place of my country is among the members of the G20”. In 2022, following the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Polish government argued that their country should replace Russia.

Last December, the US invited Poland to join this year’s summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Poland was “assuming its rightful place” at the forum.

Poland has argued that its membership is justified by its economy being on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world.

Though G20 membership is not decided solely on that basis, the G20 does include most of the world’s 20 largest economies (only Switzerland and the Netherlands have larger economies than Poland but no G20 membership).

Polish President @NawrockiKn “does not like” the fact that Donald Trump has invited Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami, says his chief foreign policy aide.

However, Nawrocki still plans to attend the event, which Poland is invited to as a guest https://t.co/JojsFB4NX6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2026

In September, the United States provoked criticism from European leaders, including Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, when it announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be invited to the Miami summit.

Subsequently, Przydacz confirmed that, although Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Trump, “does not like” the fact that Putin has been invited, the Polish president was still planning to attend the summit.

Sikorski likewise said he would attend a G20 meeting of foreign ministers in Atlanta in October even if a Russian representative was there and agreed that Poland should not boycott the summit in December.

]]> Independent beats PM Tusk’s candidate in Kraków mayoral election https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/11/independent-beats-pm-tusks-candidate-in-krakow-mayoral-election/ Sun, 11 Oct 2026 21:16:04 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105352

Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. Turnout was 44.3%.

“Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.”

The victory marks a blow for Tusk – whose Civic Coalition (KO) party has its strongest support in large cities – just a year before he seeks to win another term at parliamentary elections. The prime minister had visited Kraków to campaign alongside Piątkowska.

Dziś 11 października 2026 roku, po 24 latach, mieszkańcy odzyskali swoje miasto. Chciałbym podziękować wszystkim Krakowianom, którzy mi zaufali i zdecydowali się oddać ma mnie głos.

To nasze wspólne zwycięstwo. Dziękuję mojej partnerce Adzie, sztabowi i współpracownikom ze… pic.twitter.com/0FsNYwjPkj

— Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) October 11, 2026

For Gibała, a wealthy businessman who has largely funded his own political career, this was victory at the fourth attempt, having stood in every mayoral contest since 2014, obtaining a growing share of the vote each time.

He stood as an independent, promising to sort out the city’s finances, end cronyism in the appointment of municipal officials, improve public transport and reverse ticket-price increases, and hold a referendum on Kraków’s controversial clean transport zone for vehicles.

He also pledged to favour residents over developers in planning decisions and to counteract the negative effects of tourism in what is Poland’s most-visited city, including by restricting short-term-rental properties.

Gibała’s victory had been expected after he came top in the first round two weeks ago with 36.4% of the vote among the seven candidates who stood. Piątkowska trailed on 29.9%. The top two candidates then met in today’s run-off.

 

Piątkowska was the joint candidate of Tusk’s centrist KO party and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which are both part of the national government.

She has, since last year, been a member of the Senate in Warsaw. Previously, she worked in Kraków city hall during the mayoralty of Jacek Majchrowski, who held office from 2002 to 2024.

Piątkowska received the personal backing of Tusk, who announced her candidacy in June alongside PSL leader and deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (though critics noted that they held the event in Warsaw rather than Kraków). Tusk also visited Kraków before the first round to support his candidate.

Among her campaign promises were to seek to locate an AI “gigafactory” in Kraków, to boost the availability of housing for young people, and to implement a package of policies for women, including free mammograms, pram-friendly infrastructure, free menstrual hygiene products, and safer nighttime public transport.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Kraków’s election was held in unusual circumstances after the previous mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, also from KO, was removed from his position in May, just two years into his term. He had faced accusations of cronyism and poor financial management, as well as criticism over the introduction of the clean transport zone.

A petition to hold a recall referendum received more than the 58,355 signatures required. In the subsequent referendum, 97.3% supported removing the mayor (Miszalski had appealed to his supporters not to vote in an unsuccessful effort to keep turnout below the 27% needed for the result to be binding).

Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”.

The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party).

]]> Polish security services report alleged assassination plot against PM Tusk https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/11/polish-security-services-report-alleged-assassination-plot-against-pm-tusk/ Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:02:02 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105342

Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

At the time of writing, no details have been released regarding where and how the alleged attacks were expected to take place, who might be behind them, or what the source of the information was.

W związku z informacją, która wpłynęła do @PolskaPolicja i dotyczy możliwego zamachu na premiera @donaldtusk oraz wicepremiera, ministra obrony narodowej @KosiniakKamysz, minister koordynator służb specjalnych @TomaszSiemoniak oraz minister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji…

— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 11, 2026

On Sunday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, first announced that the police had received “information…regarding a possible assassination attempt” on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz, who, as well as serving as defence minister, is also a deputy prime minister.

Dobrzyński revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW), police and State Protection Service (SOP), which provides security for high-ranking officials, would meet to discuss the potential threat.

Speaking after that meeting, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka confirmed that the threat had first been identified by SOP, which passed the information on to the police.

 

“We are taking this matter extremely seriously,” added Dobrzyński, speaking alongside her. He criticised “pseudo-experts” in the media who had expressed doubt about the announcement of a possible assassination attempt.

“We’re talking about threats directed at the most important people in the country,” he added. “This information is so serious and credible that we’ve decided to share it with you now…We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out.”

Dobrzyński did not divulge any details about the nature of the attack or where the warnings had come from, but said that he would be able to provide further information once the police and security services had carried out further investigation.

"Sprawę traktujemy śmiertelnie poważnie. Mówimy o dużym prawdopodobieństwie spełnienia tych gróźb"

Rzecznik prasowy ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych o możliwym zamachu na premiera i szefa MON. pic.twitter.com/2xoWrZJT2w

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 11, 2026

Government spokesman Adam Szłapka, speaking to broadcaster TVN, acknowledged that the authorities constantly receive a “cascade of indications” regarding potential threats. However, “this signal was more disturbing than previous” ones, he added.

Szłapka also indicated that one element of the warning had come via email, but added that “it was not just an email” that had raised concern. Like Dobrzyński, he said that further information would be released in due course.

Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reports that an unnamed “official close to the prime minister” had said that the threat came from “right-wing extremists” and that the perpetrators were Poles.

Another source within the intelligence services told the newspaper that the threat was treated more seriously than others because it contained information about addresses linked to Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Poland has charged a 17-year-old with planning neo-Nazi terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school.

Two other Polish teenagers who were part of the same online community promoting neo-Nazism and violence have also been detained https://t.co/86AnIHWFe8

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026

Last month, police detained a 56-year-old man in the city of Przemyśl after he posted a video on social media threatening Tusk. Earlier in September, a 52-year-old man in the town of Oława was likewise arrested for making criminal threats against the prime minister online.

Also in September, the security services detained three teenagers who were accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them was additionally charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school.

This week has also seen Poland facing an unprecedented security challenge after three knife attacks took place on schools, leaving one person dead and many injured.

In response, the police have since Friday carried out checks at over 64,000 locations, including many schools, and detained over 100 people, most of them teenagers found to have made threats or been in possession of weapons.

]]> Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/09/polish-prosecutors-seek-to-drop-case-against-south-asian-men-who-slaughtered-goat-in-kebab-bar/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 13:58:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105228

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.

They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 13 Oct 2026 08:35:37 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Premier Inn owner Whitbread hits out at ‘destructive’ activist investor https://www.cityam.com/premier-inn-owner-whitbread-hits-out-at-destructive-investor-pressure/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 07:15:25 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465150

Premier Inn owner Whitbread has hit out at the activist investor seeking a seat on its board, claiming its proposals would be a “complete waste” of time and money.  The FTSE 100 hospitality firm wrote to shareholders on Tuesday urging them to reject the plans put forward by Corvex Asset Management, one of the group’s [...]]]>

Premier Inn owner Whitbread has hit out at the activist investor seeking a seat on its board, claiming its proposals would be a “complete waste” of time and money. 

The FTSE 100 hospitality firm wrote to shareholders on Tuesday urging them to reject the plans put forward by Corvex Asset Management, one of the group’s biggest shareholders. 

Corvex has accused Whitbread of “chronic misallocation of capital” and a misguided “commitment to the status quo”. The investor has called for a “rigorous, fact-based review” of the company’s strategy. 

But the Premier Inn owner hit back at the investor, claiming its recent company review resulted in “a significant evolution of Whitbread’s strategy and establishes clear and measurable commitments”.

“The board believes that duplicating the business and strategic review which has only just finished would be a complete waste of company – and shareholder – resources,” it told shareholders.

“It would also destroy the momentum we are seeing and delay and compromise the delivery of value that the Five-Year Plan is on course to create.”

Whitbread also criticised Corvex for changing its demands of the company. In May, the investor called for the group to put itself up for sale, but has more recently said it has “no pre-determined agenda” for the company’s future.

“We want to work with the board in a collegiate and non-adversarial way, as one member among many, bringing a direct shareholder perspective to these decisions,” Corvex managing partner Keith Meister said.

Whitbread takes £178m hit

Whitbread has called a general meeting on 9 November, where investors will vote on whether to appoint Corvex’s James Gemmel to the group’s board. Whitbread has urged investors to vote against this proposal.

The hospitality group revealed on Tuesday that it had taken a £178m hit to profit from its turnaround plan, which saw it sell off all of its restaurants and shed nearly 4,000 staff. The charge dragged pre-tax profit to £109m in the 12 months to the end of August, down 62 per cent on last year.

Whitbread said its new strategy is gaining pace, pointing to 4.5 per cent accommodation sales growth in the UK and Ireland and £39m in cost savings.

Chief executive Dominic Paul said: “With excellent strategic progress and strong current trading momentum, our plan is working. 

“Against this positive backdrop, the Board strongly recommends that all shareholders vote against the resolution proposed by Corvex at the forthcoming shareholder meeting.”

Plus500 has laid out plans for a “super-app” in the US after completing a takeover that will deepen its presence across the Atlantic.

The FTSE 250 fintech said on Tuesday it had begun development of a super-app that will offer “sophisticated trading capabilities” and new features for US users.

It came as the firm revealed it had bought retail investor platform Hedge, which holds a US broker-dealer registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

The London-listed group said the takeover provides the SEC-regulation needed to launch its new super-app in the US in the first quarter of 2027. It added it plans to expand to further geographies “over time”.

Plus500 began operations in the UK shortly after it was founded in 2008. It expanded into the US nearly fifteen years later following the acquisition of Cunningham Commodities in 2021.

US super-app ‘significant’ step, says Plus500 boss

In the UK, it offers contracts for difference, which allow users to speculate on price movements without owning the underlying assets, and is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority.

The fintech recorded its highest customer income growth in five years in the first half of 2026 following its broader expansion into the US.

Segments outside of its traditional over-the-counter business scaled rapidly following the launch of its event-based prediction contracts. The contracts are financial derivatives where a user pays a fixed amount on a yes-or-no outcome of a future occurrence. So far, it has mainly focused on US sporting events.

The group’s boss David Zruia said the Hedge takeover was a “pivotal step” in the firm’s US growth plan and set it up for access to the “world’s largest retail investment market”.

“With our new hub in New York and the experienced Hedge team joining us, we have the people, licences and technology to accelerate our growth and generate sustainable, long-term returns for our shareholders,” he said.

Zrui added the new super-app would be one of Plus500’s “most significant product developments”.

Bellway has warned the government’s revival of the Help to Buy scheme could further slow the housing market in the near term by encouraging housebuyers to delay decisions.

The FTSE 250 housebuilder said Labour’s new equity loan scheme, Your First Home, is a “welcome development” but cautioned it will not immediately solve the UK’s housing market slowdown. 

Jason Honeyman, chief executive of Bellway, told shareholders on Tuesday: “While the Government’s proposed Your First Home scheme has the potential to provide meaningful support for first-time buyer demand, the period ahead of its launch may influence the timing of purchasing decisions among some prospective customers.”

British housebuilders have been calling for the government to boost housing affordability as soaring mortgage rates caused by the Iran war put Brits off moving homes.

Honeyman said: “Customer demand remains constrained by affordability pressures, with mortgage interest rates above prior-year levels, while wider economic uncertainty continues to affect homebuyer decision-making.”

Bellway’s boss said these “subdued trading conditions” have plagued the sector for most of the year, adding that housebuilders are still waiting for “further detail on the scope, design and timing” of Your First Home.

Bellway sees ‘robust’ trading

The scheme will offer first-time buyers a 20 per cent equity loan towards a deposit of 2.5 per cent, with an initial interest-free period.

Andy Burnham has said the programme will help young people who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” get on the housing ladder. 

Housebuilders and property experts had long been demanding a return to the Help to Buy programme, which was set up by then-Chancellor George Osborne in 2013 but ended in 2022.

Shares in London’s listed housebuilders surged after the new scheme was announced, but some economists have cautioned that the supply-side issues caused by soaring building costs must still be addressed. 

Bellway told shareholders on Tuesday that it managed to produce a “robust” performance in the year to the end of July, despite the “ongoing challenges across the housing market”. 

The group’s total housing completions grew by 11 per cent to 9,695 homes, driving a 14 per cent uplift in revenue to £3.2bn. The firm’s pre-tax profit jumped by 22 per cent to £270m. 

“Bellway has the financial strength, operational capability and land bank to respond as market conditions improve and increase the delivery of much-needed new homes over the medium term,” Honeyman added.

BP is bracing for a hit of up to $4.5bn after a hefty write-down in its energy transition unit, as the firm pivots away from aggressive green targets. The FTSE 100 energy giant told markets on Tuesday its third quarter update – set for the end of the month – would include a post-tax impairment [...]]]>

BP is bracing for a hit of up to $4.5bn after a hefty write-down in its energy transition unit, as the firm pivots away from aggressive green targets.

The FTSE 100 energy giant told markets on Tuesday its third quarter update – set for the end of the month – would include a post-tax impairment charge in the range of $3bn to $4.5bn.

“These charges are primarily attributable to transition businesses in the gas & low carbon energy segment,” BP said.

It follows a massive scale back on green ambitions from the oil and gas major, which slashed its planned transition capital expenditure by more than $5bn annually earlier this year to a target of up to $2bn.

Alex Pugh, analyst at Freetrade, said: “BP spent years trying to reinvent itself as an energy company, and this quarter it looks set to have made its money being a very good refinery…

“Another $3bn to $4.5bn of expected write-downs, mostly on low-carbon businesses, shows the green dream still isn’t fully paid for.”

In the final quarter of 2025, it forecast write-downs of between $4bn and $5bn (£3.7bn) after the group began to rethink its strategy for transition assets and partnerships in the gas and low-carbon sector.

BP has began selling off and restructuring parts of its transition unit, including the sale of the majority of its clean-energy and transition-focused venture capital porfolio to growth investor Verdane in July 2026.

It also follows growing pressure from activist investor Elliott Management, which upped its stake to more than five per cent last year, to abandon its green commitments, slash renewable investments and ramp up fossil fuel spending.

BP in line for bumper quarter

Elsewhere, BP forecast a major reduction in its net debt to $13.5bn to $14.5bn, down from $22.3bn in the second quarter of the year.

Stronger refining margins – the difference between the cost of crude oil and the market value of finished fuels like diesel and gasoline – are also expected to deliver a $1.9 billion to $2.1 billion earnings boost compared to the previous quarter.

The margins boost follows a similar move from peer Shell, which is poised to reap major gains from the global surge in fuel prices.

Oil prices surged above the $100 mark through September due to the ongoing conflict in Iran.

BP expects its ​upstream production ​to fall between 2.19m ‌to ⁠2.24m barrels of oil equivalent per day, ​compared to ​around ⁠2.2m barrels in the previous quarter.

Last week the leaders of G7 nations agreed to release a 100m barrels of emergency diesel and oil in a bid to stave off a supply crisis. The group of advanced economies said they would work with the International Energy Agency to ramp up releases from their emergency stockpiles “in light of ongoing market pressures”.

The top brass at BP have undergone a major reshuffle over the last year following a boardroom bust-up that led to the ousting of former chair Albert Manifold in May.

Manifold’s exit was reported to have been due to his “volcanic” temper towards colleagues, which stretched to verbal abuse and bullying. Manifold has disputed the characterisation of his conduct.

It came months after former boss Murray Auchincloss departed his role as chief executive after just under two years. He was replaced by former Woodside chief executive Meg O’Neill, who formally stepped into the role in April.

O’Neil will deliver her first strategy update in New York in December.

    Did you know the Rugby League World Cup starts this week?

    If you’re reading this in the north of England then the answer is probably yes. If down south then I suspect the answer is much more likely to be no. This is a huge problem.

    Rugby league has one of the most watchable products in British sport. It is fast, physical, easy to understand and packed with elite athletes. Yet once again, as its biggest international tournament approaches, it’s trapped inside its own bubble.

    The issue is not the quality of the sport. It’s the distribution and storytelling.

    Four years ago, the 2022 Rugby League World Cup was everywhere. Every match was available through the BBC. England’s opening game against Samoa reached a substantial audience and, importantly, the tournament brought people into the sport who had not previously watched rugby league.

    This time, every match sits exclusively on Premier Sports in Britain and Ireland. That might make commercial sense in a rights negotiation, but it raises other questions.

    Such as: what is the purpose of a Rugby League World Cup?

    It’s the shop window the sport has. The moment when people who do not watch Super League every weekend are introduced to the players, the international rivalries and intensity of the sport. Putting that shop window behind a paywall reduces the chances of people discovering it.

    Rugby league needs personalities, narrative and cultural relevance

    The wider problem is that rugby league too often markets itself to people who already love rugby league.

    George Williams, Mikey Lewis, Herbie Farnworth and Jack Welsby are brilliant players. But how many casual sports fans could pick them out of a line-up? 

    The sport should be creating personalities, rivalries and storylines that mean something beyond its traditional heartlands. That’s the job for the marketing department.

    Team-wise, Australia remain the benchmark, but they are no longer untouchable. New Zealand regularly beat them, while Samoa reached the last World Cup final. Tonga have also become a genuine force and England have players performing at the highest level in both Super League and Down Under in the NRL.

    There is always jeopardy, brilliant athletes and off-field drama. We just don’t have any noise around the World Cup. 

    Where are the players on mainstream podcasts, breakfast TV and being serenaded by politicians? Where are the documentaries, creator collaborations and crossover campaigns? Where are Premier League clubs in rugby league heartlands pushing England’s World Cup campaign to their own enormous audiences?

    Sport today competes in the attention economy. Rugby league needs to build personalities, narratives and cultural relevance.

    Rugby league has spent years wondering why it does not receive the attention it deserves, but no sport deserves any attention. You must compete for it.

    With the World Cup about to begin, rugby league’s biggest challenge is not convincing its existing supporters that it matters but connecting with and convincing everyone else.

    Simon Dent is an entrepreneur and brand builder with more than 20 years’ experience. He is currently chairman of Counteruck.

    Andy Burnham earned his spurs as a great communicator on the back of a few summer TikToks, but is the shine coming off just a couple of months into the new job? While some people still appreciate the supposedly down to earth ‘tell it like it is’ approach, there can be no denying that the PM’s loose lips have got him into hot water in recent weeks. Labour sources concede that Burnham’s tendency to “shoot from the hip” is becoming a problem.

    Consider his comments on Heathrow expansion, when he said the third runway “is a matter for London” before suggesting he shouldn’t offer a view, given the proposal is currently subject to a consultation. The apparent lack of support for the multi-billion pound national infrastructure project sent panic through the sector, and saw a concerted effort from Whitehall to reassure industry figures that the government remains supportive.

    Then we had his remarkably ill-judged comments on Manchester City, where he seemed to suggest instinctive support for the club’s Abu Dhabi ownership. His aides were forced to clarify his comments.

    Most recently the PM seemed to share the details of a high-level intelligence briefing he’d asked for on Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit vote, to the delight of podcast hosts Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart. Having offered much more heat than light, his own ministers and, ultimately, the Downing Street spokesperson, spent all of Monday rowing back from the comments and clarifying that there was no evidence of such activity affecting the result of the vote.

    He seems to revel in a ‘just saying’ attitude

    Do you see the pattern here? Burnham speaks with all the confidence of a regional mayor but without the gravitas of a Prime Minister. He seems to revel in a “just saying” attitude, without recognising the consequences of his words. Time and again he lets slip a comment or a point of view that has to be clarified, rectified or disowned by his aides or ministers. The Brexit comments are particularly incendiary given that he’s on record saying (when he was trying to return to Westminster) that no good would come from opening old wounds.     Two of the world’s most senior central bankers have issued a warning that politicians would do well to heed: governments may believe they have years to repair their finances but bond markets can decide otherwise in an afternoon.     Three days later, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey reinforced the message. He warned that higher public debt and a changing investor base have made sovereign bond markets increasingly vulnerable to sudden reversals.

    The danger is not necessarily that governments cannot repay their debts, but that investors demand a sharply higher return to finance them, undermining the government’s fiscal plans. Rising debt-servicing costs then absorb more government revenue, leaving less available for public services or responding to future shocks. If investors rush to sell and market-makers cannot absorb the supply, yields can rise far beyond what underlying fundamentals justify. Fiscal sustainability is therefore not simply an exercise in projecting debt-to-GDP ratios decades into the future. It also depends on the willingness of financial markets to fund governments in the meantime.

    This is uncomfortable for politicians accustomed to treating the public finances as an accounting exercise. Fiscal rules can be adjusted, growth forecasts revised and spending commitments postponed. The mathematics might satisfy the Treasury, but it cannot guarantee the confidence of those expected to fund the borrowing.

    Across the developed world, governments face mounting demands for defence spending, ageing populations and economic investment, just as successive inflationary shocks have complicated the task of managing their debt. Britain must reconcile its spending promises with fiscal credibility; France faces political instability alongside deteriorating public finances; and even America’s reserve-currency privilege cannot indefinitely insulate Washington from the cost of borrowing.

    Politics collides with reality

    These different political circumstances are colliding with the same financial reality: governments need investors to absorb enormous debt issuance, just as the nature of those investors is changing.

    This was the second important element of Bailey’s warning. Sovereign bond markets increasingly depend on leveraged investors, whose willingness to participate depends on funding costs, volatility and their capacity to maintain positions. They provide valuable liquidity in normal conditions, but margin calls and forced selling can magnify market moves. Investors willing to finance borrowing yesterday can become sellers tomorrow.

    The UK discovered the consequences during the 2022 gilt crisis, when leveraged pension fund strategies were forced to sell assets into a falling market. The Bank of England intervened as a market-maker of last resort, temporarily purchasing government bonds to prevent disorderly trading from developing into a wider financial crisis.

    Four years later, the episode is still largely remembered as the downfall of Liz Truss. Yet focusing on the Prime Minister risks missing its more instructive lesson. The potentially most expensive measure, the original two-year Energy Price Guarantee, had been announced before Kwarteng’s mini-Budget. The crisis was not simply about the size of the fiscal commitments, but about their credibility, financing and the vulnerabilities of the gilt market.

    More importantly, the political response was remarkably swift. Tax measures were progressively reversed, the Chancellor replaced and, within weeks, the Prime Minister had resigned. The Bank’s intervention remained temporary, ending its emergency purchases on 14 October as intended. It had bought time for pension funds to reduce leverage while the political system began correcting the fiscal course.

    This was a market-functioning rescue, not an open-ended commitment to finance government borrowing. It worked because the Bank addressed a technical breakdown while the political system was moving to restore fiscal credibility.

    If yields rise because investors have lost confidence in fiscal sustainability, that is the market performing its disciplinary function. Having campaigned against austerity, he secured a decisive rejection of the proposals. Yet within days, confronted by a collapsing banking system and the prospect of leaving the euro, he agreed to a new bailout framework requiring substantial reforms.

    Britain and Greece faced very different circumstances. The UK retained monetary sovereignty and confronted a market liquidity crisis; Greece depended on external assistance and faced the possibility of leaving the single currency. What they shared was the need for political decisions to resolve pressures that financial intervention alone could not eliminate.
